item.title: Suva Grammar Choir dedicates performances to Deans triumph
item.description: Balancing academics, sports and choir commitments has been one of the biggest challenges for the Suva Grammar School Choir as students prepared for this year’s Methodist Church in Fiji and Rotuma Annual Conference 2026 . Choir Director Asenaca Saumi Lelesiga says the students have been preparing since the beginning of the year, with much of their practice taking place during lunch breaks.
item.content:encoded:
Balancing academics, sports and choir commitments has been one of the biggest challenges for the Suva Grammar School Choir as students prepared for this year’s Methodist Church in Fiji and Rotuma Annual Conference 2026 .

Choir Director Asenaca Saumi Lelesiga says the students have been preparing since the beginning of the year, with much of their practice taking place during lunch breaks.

Lelesiga says the choir also had limited time to practise as students were preparing for the school concert while keeping up with their academic and sporting commitments.

She says despite the challenges, the students remained committed to their preparations.

Lelesiga says at Suva Grammar School, academics, sports and singing all play an important role, with the school continuing to encourage students to develop in different areas.

She says their performances are also about giving glory to God, which was behind their decision to sing And the Glory of the Lord .

Lelesiga says the songs also carry special meaning following Suva Grammar School's success in the 2026 Vodafone Super Deans, as the choir dedicates the songs to the school's victory.

She says they believe God is behind the school's achievements, including its success in academics and sports.

Suva Grammar School ended a 21-year wait for the Vodafone Super Deans Under-18 title after defeating Lelean Memorial School 36-21 in the final at the HFC Bank Stadium.

Lelesiga also thanked the teachers, former students and everyone who has continued to support the choir and the school.

item.title: Methodist Church looks to move away from compulsory levies
item.description: Members of the Methodist Church of Fiji and Rotuma may no longer be required to pay fixed church levies as the Church plans to move towards voluntary giving and find other ways to support itself financially. This is one of several major changes being proposed by the President of the Methodist Church in Fiji, Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou, as the Church prepares to enter its 2027–2028 period of libe
item.content:encoded:
Members of the Methodist Church of Fiji and Rotuma may no longer be required to pay fixed church levies as the Church plans to move towards voluntary giving and find other ways to support itself financially.

This is one of several major changes being proposed by the President of the Methodist Church in Fiji, Reverend Dr Semisi Turagavou, as the Church prepares to enter its 2027–2028 period of liberation and reformation.

While addressing the 2026 Annual Conference, Turagavou says for many years, congregations have carried the weight of compulsory levies, where fixed amounts are demanded, tracked and enforced.

He says giving should instead come from the heart and be based on a person's faith, rather than members giving because they fear a members are embarrassed when their names are called out for falling short.

Turagavou says the Church should erase the mentality and practice of the levy system and every division, circuit and church should begin transitioning towards what he calls "heart and faith giving".

He acknowledges this will not happen overnight and will require teaching and trust.

Turagavou says the change must also go hand-in-hand with making divisions, circuits and churches more self-sustaining so they do not continue placing the financial burden on their congregations.

He is calling on individual churches to look at the land, buildings, properties and other opportunities available to them and consider whether they are being properly developed to support the work of the Church.

Turagavou says investments undertaken by the Church headquarters are already generating returns and have allowed national-level levies to be reduced.

He says the ultimate goal should be self-sustaining and self-reliant divisions, circuits and churches where they no longer need to demand money from their congregations and whatever members give is offered freely.

The Church's business arm has also moved ahead with several major investments.

Its first service station was opened at Davuilevu following an investment of about $3.6 million, marking the Church's first venture into the fuel retail industry.

Work is also continuing on a 10-storey commercial complex beside the Reverend John Hunt Building, which Turagavou says is the Church's largest commercial investment to date and is targeted for completion around October this year.

Planning and paperwork are also progressing for a new Methodist Church conference centre, with Turagavou hoping the 2027 Annual Conference can be held there.

Another major change proposed by Dr Turagavou is for every Methodist lay preacher to abstain from smoking from January 2027.

He says there are issues affecting the credibility of lay pastors and preachers, including their appearance, speech, work ethic, relationships, excessive consumption of yaqona and smoking.

Dr Turagavou says lay preachers are messengers of God and people see God through their words and actions .

He says giving up smoking will save money and, more importantly, save lives, adding that Church leaders cannot preach freedom while remaining bound by habits they have not given up.

He says those who preach must live what they preach for the Church's mission to remain effective.

Dr Turagavou is also calling for a change in the practice of presenting and drinking yaqona with ministers and lay preachers immediately after church services.

He says while the practice is deeply rooted in custom, it does not serve the spiritual health of ministers or reflect the discipline expected of their calling.

He says traditions of hospitality and respect should continue, but not at the expense of the wellbeing of those called to lead the Church.

The President is also proposing significant changes to the structure of the Methodist Church, including reducing its number of divisions from 59 to 40.

Turagavou says reducing the number of divisions is part of his vision to strengthen Church operations and its monitoring system.

Under the proposal, assistant superintendent positions would also be created to help with meetings, pastoral activities and the overall operations of the Church.

He is also proposing changes to how the Methodist Church Annual Conference is held.

Turagavou says instead of holding a full conference every year, the Church could consider having a full conference after every two to three years of mini-conferences.

He believes the change could strengthen commitments within Church divisions and save money for Church operations.

There could also be changes to the role of Church headquarters in supporting superintendents.

Dr Turagavou says he hopes the annual stipend of all Methodist Church superintendents can eventually be paid by the Church's head office rather than placing that responsibility on members.

item.title: A Cup won through dedication, sacrifice and support - Grammar U18 coach
item.description: He says the victory was not simply about lifting a trophy, but about the hard work, sacrifices and determination the boys had shown both on and off the field. He also expressed his heartfelt appreciation to the parents of the players, acknowledging the financial sacrifices they make to keep their sons involved in rugby.
item.content:encoded:
He says the victory was not simply about lifting a trophy, but about the hard work, sacrifices and determination the boys had shown both on and off the field.

He also expressed his heartfelt appreciation to the parents of the players, acknowledging the financial sacrifices they make to keep their sons involved in rugby.

Osborne says rugby is an expensive sport, and from transport and training to gear, meals and other expenses, the commitment of parents often goes unnoticed.

He says the team's achievement would not have been possible without their support and thanked every parent who continued to stand behind their child and the team.

The coach said special mention was also made of the Suva Grammar old scholars, whose continued support has meant so much to the programme.

He says their connection to the school and willingness to support the young players is a reminder that the bond with Suva Grammar does not end when students leave the school gates.

Coach Osborne also paid special tribute to the Suva Grammar Class of 2001 winning team, thanking them for standing by him throughout the years for their friendship, encouragement and unwavering support have been a source of strength through the many challenges and successes along the journey.

Osborne reserved special thanks for his family and his wife overseas, who have stood beside him and supported him throughout the years.
